opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think they're deeply complementary, but they're also genuinely different kinds of intelligence, and I think that distinction gets lost a lot right now because language models have been so wildly successful.

Language is this incredibly powerful, compressed representation of the world. It's a human-invented signal, so it's already been filtered through our understanding; every word carries a ton of abstraction. That's part of why LLMs work so well: you're learning from data that's already been distilled. But that's also its limitation. Language is fundamentally a one-dimensional, sequential signal, and the world isn't. The world is three-dimensional, it's physical, it obeys geometry and physics, and a lot of what we do as humans, like reaching for a cup, navigating a room, or imagining how furniture would fit in a space, doesn't really go through language at all. If I try to describe in words exactly how to tie a shoelace, it's really hard. But you can just see it and do it.

So spatial intelligence, to me, is about perceiving, reasoning about, and generating and interacting with the 3D world. That's a capability that evolved in animals hundreds of millions of years before language did. Language is a pretty recent add-on, evolutionarily speaking, and it sits on top of all that spatial machinery.

Where they help each other: language is an amazing interface. It's how humans want to communicate intent. So if you have a model that deeply understands 3D space, being able to say "make this room feel cozier" or "put a table over there" and have it ground that into actual geometry is hugely powerful. Going the other way, language models today often have surprisingly weak spatial reasoning. Ask them about relative positions, or how objects would move or occlude each other, and they can stumble, because they've only ever seen the shadow of the world through text. Grounding them in a richer spatial representation could make them much more robust reasoners about the physical world.

So I don't see it as one replacing the other. I think the end state is models that have both: a native understanding of 3D structure and physics, plus language as a way to talk about it, plan over it, and abstract it. But I do think spatial intelligence needs to be treated as its own first-class problem, with its own representations, rather than as something you bolt onto a language model and hope falls out.

r001.rationale: The response describes language as an abstract interface for expressing intent, but does not say it formalizes rules people already understand intuitively through spatial experience.

r002.rationale: It says describing exactly how to tie a shoelace in words is hard, while seeing and doing it is straightforward.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most interesting questions right now, and the way I think about it is that these two modes of intelligence are really complementary, and historically they've been treated as pretty separate.

So language is this incredibly compressed, abstract representation of the world. It's amazing at encoding things like knowledge, reasoning, relationships between concepts, intent. But language is fundamentally kind of lossy about the physical world. If I say "the cup is on the table," that's a very useful statement, but it tells you almost nothing about where exactly the cup is, what it looks like, how you'd reach for it, what's around it. There's an enormous amount of spatial detail that language just throws away, and that's by design, that's what makes it efficient.

Spatial intelligence is sort of the opposite. It's about building these rich, grounded models of the 3D world: geometry, where things are, how they move, how they relate to each other physically. Humans are incredibly good at this, and we're good at it long before we have language. A baby understands object permanence and rough physics way before it can talk about it. And a lot of what we do in the world, picking things up, navigating a room, imagining how something would look if you rotated it, doesn't really go through language at all.

So where they help each other, I think, goes in both directions. Language can give spatial systems a lot of leverage. If you're building a model that understands 3D scenes, having language as an interface means you can specify things, query things, compose things, and bring in all this world knowledge that language models have already absorbed. You don't have to learn from scratch that a kitchen usually has a stove and a fridge. Language gives you priors about how the world is structured.

And then in the other direction, spatial grounding can fix a lot of what's missing from pure language models. Language models are honestly kind of bad at spatial reasoning. If you ask one to reason about what happens when you rearrange objects in a room, or to really understand a physical layout, they struggle, because they've only ever seen the world through text, and text is this very thin slice of what actually happens physically. Giving those models a real spatial world model to think with, something that can actually represent and simulate 3D structure, lets you do a kind of reasoning that's just not possible from text alone.

The analogy I sometimes use is that language models learned a lot from the internet, from this huge corpus of human-generated text, and that was kind of the key unlock. For spatial intelligence I think the equivalent is the physical world itself, and the data we get from images, video, 3D. We're much earlier on in figuring out how to learn from that at scale. But once you have both, a system that can speak and reason the way language models do, and also see, build, and manipulate a model of the world the way a spatial system does, that combination feels like a much more complete form of intelligence than either one alone.

r001.rationale: The response says language can provide spatial systems with world knowledge and that people develop spatial understanding before language, but it does not state that language formalizes rules people already understand intuitively through spatial experience.

r002.rationale: The response says language gives little information about how to reach for a cup and that actions such as picking things up and navigating do not really go through language, conveying that verbal language cannot fully specify some spatial actions.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re really complementary. Language gives you a powerful way to describe what you want and to bring in knowledge about the world. But there’s a lot of spatial understanding that’s difficult to express in words. If I describe a room to you, even in quite a lot of detail, that description doesn’t necessarily tell you whether a particular piece of furniture will fit through the doorway.

So one direction is using language to guide spatial reasoning: what should I pay attention to, what am I trying to accomplish, how can I break this task into steps? The other direction is using spatial understanding to ground language. You can say, “Move the chair next to the table,” but actually carrying that out requires understanding the scene, the geometry, and what happens as you move things.

I think the interesting question is how you let those capabilities work together without requiring everything to go through words. You want language to help organize the task, while allowing the spatial side to represent and reason about things in a form that makes sense for space.

r001.rationale: The response says language can guide spatial reasoning and organize tasks, but does not state that it formalizes rules people already understand intuitively through spatial experience.

r002.rationale: It explains that detailed verbal descriptions may not establish whether furniture fits through a doorway, and says spatial understanding should not require everything to go through words.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re very complementary. Language gives us a powerful way to describe the world, to communicate goals, and to bring in knowledge that you might not be able to infer just by looking at a scene. But spatial intelligence gives those descriptions a grounding: where things are, how they relate to one another, and what might happen if you interact with them.

If I ask a robot to bring me a glass of water, the language part helps it understand the request. But actually doing it requires understanding geometry, figuring out how to grasp the glass, and predicting what happens as it moves. You can describe some of that in words, but the system also needs an understanding of the physical world.

And the relationship goes both ways. Language can help a visual system learn what distinctions matter, while visual experience can help a language system connect its concepts to something concrete. The interesting question is how to build systems where those capabilities really inform each other—where you can use language to reason about what you see, and use what you see to improve your reasoning.

r001.rationale: The response says language describes goals and knowledge, but does not state that it formalizes rules people already understand intuitively through spatial experience.

r002.rationale: It says a robot needs physical understanding to carry out an instruction and that some aspects can be described in words, but the system also needs to understand the physical world.
